Let’s dive into Chapter Nine—Essentialism in Relationships and Teams.
You know, essentialism isn’t just about how you manage your own priorities. It can completely transform the way you connect with others and how you work together as a group. When a team or even just two people really embrace this mindset, things get clearer, collaboration feels smoother, and everyone gets more done with less stress.
So, what does essentialism look like in your relationships? Well, it’s all about investing your time and energy in the people who matter most. Instead of trying to keep up with dozens of acquaintances, you focus on your closest friends, your family, maybe a few trusted colleagues. This kind of depth makes those relationships so much more rewarding—and you feel more supported, too.
Here are a few ways you can practice essentialism with the people you care about:
First, try scheduling regular time with those important folks—put it on the calendar so it actually happens. When you’re with them, be fully present. That means setting aside your phone and tuning in to the conversation. And don’t forget to talk openly about what matters to you, and where your boundaries are. It’s amazing how much difference that honesty can make.
Now, let’s talk about essentialism in teams. When everyone is clear on what’s most important, it’s so much easier to stay focused and make real progress. Leaders have a special role here—they set the tone by protecting the team from distractions and showing what it means to focus on what really counts.
Teams can put essentialism into practice by doing a few things: set clear, shared priorities so everyone knows what matters most. Try to keep the number of active projects low, so you avoid overwhelm. And when it comes to celebrating success, focus on the really important wins, instead of spreading praise too thin.
Here’s a real-life example: imagine a company that decided to cut back on the number of projects teams were juggling. Instead of spreading themselves too thin, they zeroed in on just a handful of high-impact projects. The result? Better outcomes, happier teams, and way less burnout.
So, what’s the big takeaway? Essentialism in relationships and teams is all about quality over quantity. When you invest in the vital few—whether people or projects—you build stronger bonds, more trust, and you get results that really matter.
